## Proof

**Answer: Yes.** The path-connected component of the identity in $\text{Homeo}(M)$ acts transitively on any connected topological manifold $M$ without boundary.

### Step 1: $\text{Homeo}_0(M)$ is a subgroup

$M$ is locally compact Hausdorff, so $\text{Homeo}(M)$ with the compact-open topology is a topological group. The path-connected component of the identity, $\text{Homeo}_0(M)$, is a (normal) subgroup. In particular, if $f, g \in \text{Homeo}_0(M)$ with isotopies $f_t, g_t$ from the identity, then $g \circ f \in \text{Homeo}_0(M)$ via the isotopy $h_t = g_t \circ f_t$.

### Step 2: Local transitivity

**Claim:** For every $p \in M$, there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $p$ such that for every $q \in U$, there exists $h \in \text{Homeo}_0(M)$ with $h(p) = q$.

Choose a coordinate chart $\phi: V \to \mathbb{R}^n$ with $p \in V$, $\phi(p) = 0$. Let $B_r \subset \phi(V)$ be an open ball. Set $U = \phi^{-1}(B_{r/3})$.

Given $q \in U$, let $v = \phi(q) \in B_{r/3}$, so $|v| < r/3$. Choose $\epsilon$ with $|v| < \epsilon < (r - |v|)/2$; this is possible since $|v| < r/3$ gives $(r-|v|)/2 > r/3 > |v|$.

Define a Lipschitz bump function $\lambda: \mathbb{R}^n \to [0,1]$ by:
$$\lambda(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & |x| \le \epsilon \\ 2 - |x|/\epsilon & \epsilon < |x| \le 2\epsilon \\ 0 & |x| > 2\epsilon \end{cases}$$
This has Lipschitz constant $L = 1/\epsilon < 1/|v|$, and support in $\overline{B_{2\epsilon}} \subset B_r$.

Define $\psi_t(x) = x + t\,\lambda(x)\,v$ for $t \in [0,1]$.

**Each $\psi_t$ is a homeomorphism:** For $x \neq y$:
$$|\psi_t(x) - \psi_t(y)| \ge |x-y| - t\,|\lambda(x)-\lambda(y)|\,|v| \ge |x-y|(1 - L|v|) > 0,$$
so $\psi_t$ is injective. It is continuous and equals the identity outside $\overline{B_{2\epsilon}}$, hence is proper. By invariance of domain, $\psi_t(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is open; by properness it is also closed; by connectedness of $\mathbb{R}^n$ and nonemptiness, $\psi_t$ is surjective. Thus $\psi_t$ is a homeomorphism.

**Isotopy properties:** $\psi_0 = \mathrm{id}$, $\psi_1(0) = 0 + 1 \cdot \lambda(0) \cdot v = v$, and $(t,x) \mapsto \psi_t(x)$ is continuous with uniformly bounded support, so $t \mapsto \psi_t$ is continuous in the compact-open topology.

**Transfer to $M$:** Since $\psi_t$ is supported in $B_r \subset \phi(V)$, the map $h_t = \phi^{-1} \circ \psi_t \circ \phi$ (extended by the identity outside $V$) defines an isotopy of $M$ from the identity to a homeomorphism $h$ with $h(p) = q$. Thus $h \in \text{Homeo}_0(M)$.

### Step 3: Global transitivity

$M$ is locally Euclidean, hence locally path-connected. A connected, locally path-connected space is path-connected (standard result: the path-component of any point is both open and closed).

Given $p, q \in M$, let $\gamma: [0,1] \to M$ be a path from $p$ to $q$. By compactness of $\gamma([0,1])$, cover it by finitely many neighborhoods $U_1, \dots, U_k$ as in Step 2. Choose points $p = p_0, p_1, \dots, p_k = q$ along $\gamma$ with $p_{i-1}, p_i \in U_i$.

By Step 2, for each $i$ there exists $h_i \in \text{Homeo}_0(M)$ with $h_i(p_{i-1}) = p_i$. Since $\text{Homeo}_0(M)$ is a subgroup:
$$h = h_k \circ h_{k-1} \circ \cdots \circ h_1 \in \text{Homeo}_0(M), \quad h(p) = q.$$

Therefore $\text{Homeo}_0(M)$ acts transitively on $M$. $\blacksquare$
